hook.text: Two methods of measuring the universe's expansion rate give different answers. The disagreement is called the Hubble Tension.

buildup.text: Measuring nearby supernovae gives a faster rate. Measuring the cosmic microwave background gives a slower one.

discovery.text: The discrepancy is now statistically significant—over 5 sigma. It's not a simple measurement error anymore.

twist.text: Solving it may require new physics—perhaps a new particle, a change in dark energy, or something we haven't imagined yet.

climax.text: JWST, DESI, and Euclid are all collecting data that could resolve or deepen the tension. The answer is coming.

punchline.text: The universe can't expand at two speeds. Something in our understanding is wrong.

quiz.question: What is the Hubble Tension?
options: Two methods of measuring the universe's expansion rate give significantly different answers
A disagreement about whether the Hubble Space Telescope or JWST produces better images
The tension between gravity and dark energy that determines the universe's shape

details.summary: The Hubble tension is a growing discrepancy in measurements of the universe's expansion rate. Observations of the nearby universe give a rate of about 73 km/s/Mpc, while measurements from the early universe predict about 67. This 9% gap may signal new physics beyond the standard cosmological model.
details.whyItMatters: If the Hubble tension is real, it could mean our standard model of cosmology is incomplete. Resolving it may require new particles, modified dark energy, or revisions to fundamental physics.
takeaways: Nearby and early-universe expansion rate measurements disagree
The gap is about 9%, well beyond measurement uncertainty
Could indicate new physics beyond the standard model

faq.question: How is the expansion rate measured in two different ways?
faq.answer: Locally: using Cepheid variable stars and Type Ia supernovae as distance ladders to measure galaxy recession speeds (73 km/s/Mpc). From the early universe: analyzing the cosmic microwave background with the Planck satellite and extrapolating forward using the standard model (67km/s/Mpc).

faq.question: Could it just be a measurement error?
faq.answer: Increasingly unlikely. Both methods have been refined extensively, and the James Webb Space Telescope confirmed the local measurements in 2023. Multiple independent local techniques (gravitational lensing, tip of the red giant branch) also give higher values. The tension appears to be real.
